b: Alibaba Group's customer management revenue, the line that records what merchants pay its Taobao and Tmall marketplaces, fell 5% to RMB75.0 billion (US$11.2 billion) in the three months ended September 30, 2026, while revenue from its AI Cloud and Compute Services segment rose 53% to RMB61.0 billion. Sales and marketing expenses dropped 38% to RMB41.3 billion, partly because subsidies once counted as marketing costs are now deducted from revenue, according to results the company announced in Hong Kong on November 19, 2026, and furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission as Exhibit 99.1 to a Form 6-K.

Alibaba's group revenue grew 10% to RMB271.5 billion in the September quarter, but the fees it collects from sellers on Taobao and Tmall fell 5%, and the growth came from its cloud and AI business and from quick delivery services. The drop in seller fees is mostly an accounting effect: Alibaba now subtracts some subsidies from revenue instead of counting them as marketing costs, and without that change the line would have grown 1%. For brands and agencies that buy media on Taobao and Tmall, the numbers describe a marketplace whose merchant income is flat, a company spending far less on reported marketing, and a new AI agent, QwenWork E-commerce, designed to automate advertising and other tasks for sellers.

All figures come from Alibaba Group's results announcement for the quarter and six months ended September 30, 2026, unless marked with an asterisk as a PPC Land calculation. Percentage changes without an asterisk are the company's own, which Alibaba says are calculated on exact amounts. The release converts renminbi at RMB6.7045 to US$1.00, the Federal Reserve H.10 rate for September 30, 2026. The September quarter is the second quarter of Alibaba's fiscal year 2027.

Merchant revenue and the subsidy reclassification

Customer management revenue is the closest thing Alibaba publishes to an advertising number for its domestic marketplaces. It does not separate marketing services from other merchant charges, and it is not comparable line for line with the advertising revenue of Amazon or Meta. In the September quarter it came to RMB75,033 million, against RMB78,855 million a year earlier, a decline of RMB3.8 billion.

The release explains the gap between that figure and Alibaba's own preferred view in one sentence: "Excluding the contra revenue impact from the new business development program, customer management revenue on a like-for-like basis would have grown by 1% year-over-year." The same wording covers the six months ended September 30, when the line fell 6% to RMB157.6 billion. Alibaba's June quarter announcement of August 20, 2026, had reported a 7% decline and the same 1% like-for-like growth.

What the program is, the release does not say. Its only description sits in the explanation of sales and marketing costs, which fell "primarily due to more efficient investment in Taobao Instant Commerce and the impact of our new business development program, where relevant subsidies previously recorded as sales and marketing expenses are now recorded as contra revenue item." Cost of revenue as a share of revenue also rose, to 62.0% from 60.8%, which Alibaba attributes in part to "the contra revenue impact from the new business development program."
How the reclassification moves the numbers
According to the release, the change works through three lines of the income statement:
Subsidies that Alibaba previously recorded as sales and marketing expenses are now recorded as a contra revenue item, which reduces reported revenue.
Customer management revenue therefore falls on a reported basis. Alibaba states that, excluding the program, the line would have grown 1% in the quarter and 1% over six months.
Sales and marketing expenses fall by a matching amount, on top of the reduction Alibaba attributes to "more efficient investment in Taobao Instant Commerce."

Alibaba gives no renminbi figure for the contra revenue. A rough estimate is possible from the two growth rates: a 1% increase on RMB78.9 billion would have produced about RMB79.6 billion, so the program reduced the quarter's customer management revenue by something in the region of RMB4 billion to RMB5 billion, once rounding of the published percentages is allowed for*. On the same arithmetic, the six-month effect is in the region of RMB11 billion to RMB13 billion*. Neither estimate comes from Alibaba.

That matters for anyone reading the 38% fall in sales and marketing expenses. The line dropped by RMB25.2 billion*, to RMB41.3 billion, and fell to 15.2% of revenue from 26.8%. Only a part of that is the subsidies that moved into contra revenue; the rest, on Alibaba's description, comes from spending less to win orders in Taobao Instant Commerce. Excluding share-based compensation, sales and marketing costs fell to 15.1% of revenue from 26.6%.

The note on revenue by type in the Hong Kong version of the announcement gives a wider view. Revenue from customer management services across the whole group, which includes marketplaces outside China, was RMB217.1 billion in the six months, down 2.8%* from RMB223.4 billion. Over the same period, cloud services revenue rose 55.6%* to RMB82.2 billion and sales of goods rose 17.1%* to RMB127.0 billion. Customer management revenue from China E-commerce made up 27.6%* of group revenue in the September quarter, against 31.8%* a year earlier.

The release gives no gross merchandise value, no take rate and no split between search, display and commission income, so it is not possible to say whether merchants spent more or less on Taobao and Tmall advertising in the quarter. The like-for-like 1% is the only underlying growth figure Alibaba offers.
Against other Chinese platforms and Western retail media

The pattern of shrinking marketing budgets runs through China's large platforms this autumn. JD.com cut its marketing expenses by 26.2% to RMB15.5 billion in the September quarter as losses in its food delivery business narrowed by more than half, while its marketplace and marketing revenues rose 9.6% to RMB28.1 billion. Baidu's online marketing revenue fell 22% to RMB11.9 billion as its AI cloud infrastructure revenue rose 94%. Alibaba's reported decline in customer management revenue is smaller than Baidu's, but unlike JD's merchant income it is not growing.

Western comparisons show the scale. At US$11.2 billion, Alibaba's quarterly customer management revenue sits below the US$19.64 billion that Amazon reported in advertising revenue for the same quarter, up 11%, and far below Meta's US$63.06 billion in advertising revenue, up 26%. Alibaba's line is not limited to advertising, so the gap in pure advertising is likely wider than these figures suggest, although the release does not allow that to be measured.
QwenWork E-commerce: an agent that runs merchant advertising

The most direct change for sellers is a product rather than a number. Alibaba says it launched QwenWork E-commerce for merchants in October 2026, describing it as "an AI product powered by our agentic AI capabilities." According to the release, the product works as follows:
It sits inside QwenWork, which Alibaba calls "our one-stop AI agent platform."
It is "designed to automate end-to-end merchant workflows, including store operations, business analytics, advertising and customer service."
It "connects directly to Taobao and Tmall data" by drawing on Alibaba's existing merchant tools.
It "will further support data access across other platforms, enabling more seamless cross-platform operations." The release gives no date or list of platforms for that step.

On the earnings call, Chief Executive Eddie Wu said: "We recently launched QwenWork E-Commerce, and the percentage of paying e-commerce users continues to rise." He gave no price, user count or share of merchants. Chief Financial Officer Toby Xu said on the call that the product "is able to automate end-to-end cross-platform operations for e-commerce merchants," according to a transcript published by Investing.com.

On the shopper side, Alibaba says the Qwen model family's multimodal capabilities help it "better understand complex consumer needs and deliver more relevant product recommendations with knowledge-based reasoning." The release adds: "These enhanced capabilities have driven a notable increase in general knowledge-related queries, creating more opportunities to identify latent consumer demand, facilitate product discovery, and drive sales conversion." No query volumes or conversion figures accompany the claim.

Automated bidding on Taobao is not new. In June 2026, PPC Land reported that Alibaba's Bid2X model lifted GMV by 4.65% on Taobao in a two-month online test covering about one million campaigns. QwenWork E-commerce moves the automation from bidding to the wider set of tasks a merchant's operations team performs, advertising included, which raises the question of how much budget control sellers keep when an agent built by the platform also manages their campaigns on that platform. The release does not address it.
Shoppers, members and the consumption climate

Alibaba tracks its highest-spending customers through 88VIP, its membership program. The number of members "continued to increase by double digits year-over-year to approximately 66 million as of September 30, 2026," up from approximately 64 million at June 30, according to the June quarter announcement. The release says the ARPU of new 88VIP members, "defined as those who joined the membership program within the past year, increased significantly year-over-year during the 11.11 Global Shopping Festival." No figure is given.

Xianyu, the second-hand marketplace, grew daily active users by 23% and paid orders by 29%, according to the release, which credits AI features "including smart pricing, automated product listing descriptions and precise buyer targeting."

The outlook for the December quarter, which includes the 11.11 festival, was cautious. Asked about Taobao and Tmall on the call, Jiang Fan, Chief Executive of Alibaba E-commerce Business Group, answered in Chinese. The Investing.com transcript prints the English interpretation of his answers under Eddie Wu's name, but the Chinese text it carries is attributed to Jiang. Through the interpreter, he said: "Consumers are becoming more cautious in their spending, and certain categories continue to face intense competition. Quarter to date, our key operating metrics have been in line with the trend of national online physical goods retail sales." He added that "consumer staples are showing healthier growth than discretionary products."
Quick commerce: more revenue, smaller losses

Alibaba's quick commerce segment, China Quick Commerce, combines Taobao Instant Commerce, the Freshippo grocery chain and the on-demand delivery business of Tmall Supermarket. Revenue rose 22% to RMB58.8 billion, "primarily driven by Freshippo," and rose 10.2%* from the June quarter. Year-on-year growth slowed from 45.1%* in the June quarter.

Alibaba does not publish a loss figure for the business. The release says Taobao Instant Commerce "continued to improve its unit economics quarter-over-quarter while maintaining market share," driven by higher average order value and "an increasing focus on high-value food and non-food categories." Adjusted EBITA at Alibaba E-commerce Group rose 243% to RMB38.9 billion, "primarily driven by a significant loss reduction in the China Quick Commerce business." The segment's adjusted EBITA margin rose to 19.7%* from 5.9%, although its adjusted EBITA was 2.3% lower than in the June quarter.

Jiang Fan said on the call, through the interpreter, that gross transaction value in the online non-food categories of quick commerce "grew more than 40% year-over-year, outpacing the industry." The Chinese text in the transcript gives 40% without the words "more than." He also set out targets: "We remain committed to our goal of halving losses next year and achieving profitability in instant retail by fiscal year 2029."

The base effect is large. A year earlier, in the September quarter of 2025, group adjusted EBITA had fallen to RMB9.1 billion from RMB38.8 billion* in the June quarter of 2025. The 260% growth in the latest quarter is measured against that low point, and Alibaba's explanation for it starts with improved results at Taobao Instant Commerce.
International commerce and the European bill

International E-commerce revenue fell 8% to RMB25.7 billion, "primarily due to the decrease in revenue of AliExpress, as impacted by the EU Customs Reform, and partly offset by the revenue growth from Trendyol." The release does not define the reform. On July 1, 2026, the European Union ended the EUR150 duty exemption and started charging EUR3 per item on low-value parcels, a measure that EU finance ministers had agreed to accelerate in November 2025. Advertisers saw the effect elsewhere: Pinterest told investors in August that Asia-based cross-border retailers hit by European regulation had pulled back, and in October it put the drag at roughly 11 points of Europe's revenue growth. Pinterest did not name the retailers.

Europe also shows up in Alibaba's costs. General and administrative expenses for the six months rose to 4.2% of revenue from 3.0%, "primarily due to a provision in relation to the fine imposed by the European Commission under the Digital Services Act of EUR550 million recorded this year." The Commission fined AliExpress EUR550 million in July 2026 over its handling of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products. The release does not state the provision in renminbi or say in which quarter it was booked. AliExpress had already faced data-transfer complaints from the privacy group noyb in January 2025.

Global Wholesale, which includes Alibaba's business-to-business marketplaces, grew revenue 6% to RMB14.3 billion on cross-border value-added services. During the quarter Alibaba merged the management of its domestic and international wholesale businesses.
AI Cloud: 53% growth and a 14.5% margin

The cloud segment, which since the June quarter combines Cloud Intelligence Group with the T-Head chip unit, produced most of the group's revenue growth. Its revenue rose by RMB21.1 billion*, against an increase of RMB23.7 billion* in group revenue, although the segment figure includes sales to other Alibaba businesses. The release breaks the segment down in billions of renminbi:
AI Cloud and Compute Services (RMB bn)

Alibaba notes that the rounded values do not sum to the total. It defines recurring revenue as "ongoing, predictable revenue generated from products or services that customers purchase on a pay-as-you-go basis or through monthly or annual subscriptions," mainly public cloud services and license and software renewals. AI-related product revenue of RMB17,918 million marked the thirteenth consecutive quarter of triple-digit growth. On the call, Wu said these products "accounted for 49% of Alibaba Cloud's external recurring revenue" and that their annual revenue run rate exceeded US$10 billion; Xu put the run rate at CNY 71.7 billion.

Segment adjusted EBITA rose 121% to RMB8.8 billion. Xu's quote in the release puts the margin at 14.5%, which matches PPC Land's calculation from the segment table. Asked about margins, Wu pointed to pricing: "It puts us in a stronger bargaining position when it comes to pricing with customers, which again has contributed to a better gross margin than last year, for example." The customers named in the release include AI labs doing training and inference, and companies in the internet, automotive, embodied AI, financial services and biotechnology sectors. The release also says Alibaba Cloud was named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Strategic Cloud Platform Services, "making it the first and only Asia-Pacific provider to receive this distinction."

Alibaba's cloud remains small next to the US hyperscalers in spending terms. Its capital expenditures of US$7.5 billion in the quarter compare with the US$51.4 billion that Alphabet spent over the same three months.
Chips, export rules and a lower growth target

The results arrived three days after a change in US export policy. The Hong Kong announcement records, under subsequent events, that on November 16, 2026, the Bureau of Industry and Security of the U.S. Department of Commerce "issued an interim final rule addressing remote access to advanced semiconductors." It continues: "The Rule, as written, will impact our company's ability to access compute from certain providers outside China." Alibaba says it is evaluating the rule, "which may still be subject to change," and that "an estimate of the financial effect cannot be reasonably made as of the date of this results announcement."

On the call, Wu translated that uncertainty into a lower range for the next fiscal year, which runs from April 2027 to March 2028: "we might expect our growth target for cloud revenue to be in the 30%-45% range." He added that growth should "rebound to 50% or higher in calendar year 2028" as domestic chip output expands. The long-term target did not change: "achieving $100 billion in external cloud revenue with a margin exceeding 20%" in calendar 2030. The data center plan may shrink, however. "Based on our current preliminary assessment, it may lead to a downward revision of that long-term 20 GW target," Wu said.

Alibaba's answer is T-Head. At its Apsara Conference in September, the company unveiled the Zhenwu V900 chip for training and inference, "with commercial release scheduled for the first quarter of 2027," and open-sourced T-Head SAIL, the software stack for its Zhenwu chips. The Zhenwu M890 supernode instance launched in August; the release describes it as "China's first supernode architecture capable of supporting inference for models with more than two trillion parameters." Wu said on the call that the V900 "delivers three times the computing performance of the M890" and that large-scale production of a further chip, the J900, is planned for 2028. Asked about compliance, he said: "we have obtained and used compute in compliance with applicable laws and regulations, and of course, we will continue to do so."

T-Head's own listing is under way. The chip unit filed confidentially for a Hong Kong listing on September 11, 2026, which Alibaba disclosed on November 10. Wu told analysts: "Given listing compliance requirements, we are unable to disclose T-Head's financial information or other non-public information at this stage." Google, for comparison, said in November that its own AI chip business was nearing 100 customers.
Models and apps: a RMB10.5 billion loss

AI Labs and Applications, which brings together Alibaba's model labs, the Qwen consumer business and QwenWork, grew revenue 51% to RMB4.4 billion "primarily driven by rising demand for agentic AI products." Its adjusted EBITA loss widened to RMB10.5 billion from RMB3.4 billion, "primarily due to our increased investment in AI capabilities, and higher inference cost related to Qwen app." The loss was smaller than the June quarter's RMB13.9 billion*.

Xu linked part of that improvement to promotion: "We observed improved efficiency in both model training and marketing spend on the Qwen APP." Wu framed it as a choice. "So we've been very restrained when it comes to promotion and subsidies," he said, arguing that "if an app isn't built on a stronger, better, more unique model, if all the apps are basically running on the same model, then those apps are very easy to replicate."

The release lists the model and app launches. Qwen4-Max is "built on the new mixture-of-experts architecture with 2.4 trillion backbone parameters and native visual capabilities." The Qwen app covers "more than 20 service categories, including shopping, local services, travel, work, learning, personal finance and health," and in October gained Qwen Go!, "a cloud-based personal agent" that "autonomously executes multi-step tasks across platforms." No user numbers are given for either. Wu also said on the call that "Apple Intelligence, which is deeply integrated with Qwen, is set to launch for users in China in December," and that the company remains "very confident in achieving our target of CNY 30 billion in ARR for the full fiscal year" in its model-as-a-service business, despite model releases that "lagged a bit behind our own original expectation." Outside China, Qwen models were already part of the open-weight set that Ecosia moved to when it dropped Mistral in October.

In All others, which includes Alibaba Health, Hujing Digital Media and Entertainment Group, Amap and Lingxi Games, revenue fell 5% to RMB27.7 billion on lower Cainiao revenue, and the adjusted EBITA loss widened to RMB3.3 billion. Amap, the mapping and local services app, recorded "an all-time high of approximately 370 million peak daily active users" on October 1, 2026, the first day of China's National Day holiday.

Capital expenditures reached RMB50.5 billion (US$7.5 billion), up 60% from RMB31.5 billion. Alibaba attributes the increase to "an acceleration in scaling compute capacity, higher pricing of a broad range of chip components, an increase in CPU-compute capacity driven by anticipated growing customer adoption of AI agents, and fluctuations in procurement cycles." Spending was lower than the June quarter's RMB67.7 billion, which Xu put down to procurement timing.

Free cash flow was an outflow of RMB34.5 billion, against an outflow of RMB21.8 billion a year earlier, and RMB79.1 billion over six months. Wu told analysts that "in calendar years 2027, 2028, we will be investing most aggressively in the ramping up of our domestic chips" and that the company "should be able to achieve positive cash flow overall by 2028 in the second half of that year."

To fund the build-out, Alibaba issued 710,000,000 new shares in August 2026 at HK$112.70 each, raising HK$80.0 billion gross and about HK$79.7 billion net, according to the Hong Kong announcement. Cash and other liquid investments stood at RMB487.9 billion on September 30, down from RMB520.8 billion on March 31. Total debts to total capital fell to 17.83% from 18.86%. Xu put the net cash position at US$32.9 billion on the call. Share repurchases were modest: 31.3 million shares for US$383 million in June and July, all on the New York Stock Exchange and all since cancelled, with none reported for August or September. The board did not recommend an interim dividend.

Net income tripled to RMB64.4 billion, but most of the increase came from investments rather than operations. Interest and investment income rose to RMB73.3 billion from RMB20.1 billion, "primarily attributable to the increase in net gain from mark-to-market changes of our equity investments," and the reconciliation table lists RMB87.1 billion of gains on deemed disposals, disposals and revaluation of investments in the quarter. The release does not name the investments. Income tax expenses rose to RMB37.1 billion from RMB5.6 billion, an effective rate of 36.9%* on pre-tax income. Excluding those items, non-GAAP net income rose 92% to RMB19.9 billion.

Over six months the picture is less favorable. Non-GAAP net income fell 7% to RMB40.6 billion and non-GAAP diluted earnings per ADS fell 13%, after a goodwill impairment of RMB4.5 billion in the All others segment and the European fine provision. The company had 133,073 employees on September 30, 908* more than on June 30.

The Investing.com coverage of the call, which says it was "generated with the support of AI and reviewed by an editor," departs from the release in several places. Its summary reports "adjusted EBITDA jumping 260% to CNY 32.6 billion" and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 14.5%; in the release, RMB32.6 billion and 260% describe adjusted EBITA, adjusted EBITDA rose 167% to RMB46.1 billion with a 17% margin, and 14.5% is the cloud segment's EBITA margin. The transcript uses "EBITDA" for segment EBITA throughout and has Xu putting the cloud margin at 14.9%, against 14.5% in his written quote and in the segment table. Investing.com converts revenue to "about $40.8 billion"; the release gives US$40,498 million. It labels the quarter "Q2 2026," whereas Alibaba calls it the September quarter, the second quarter of fiscal 2027. The release schedules the next-generation supernode for the first quarter of 2027, while Wu said on the call that V900 supernode clusters "will launch at commercial scale in the second quarter of 2027."
What it means for advertisers and sellers

For brands that buy media on Taobao and Tmall, the September quarter offers less information than it appears to. The reported 5% fall in customer management revenue is driven by an accounting choice that nets subsidies against merchant income, and Alibaba's 1% like-for-like figure suggests that merchant spending on the marketplaces was roughly flat. That is slower than the 9.6% growth in JD's marketplace and marketing revenue over the same three months, and it comes with no breakdown of advertising inside the line.

The more consequential shift may be in who operates campaigns. With QwenWork E-commerce automating "store operations, business analytics, advertising and customer service" for merchants, and with promised access to data "across other platforms," Alibaba is building an agent that sits between sellers and the ad products Alibaba sells them. Combined with a 38% fall in reported marketing spend, a promise to halve quick commerce losses and a cloud business growing more than five times as fast as group revenue, the results describe a company directing its money towards compute and away from subsidies.
What the documents do not say

The release does not define the new business development program, give its start date or quantify the contra revenue, and it provides no gross merchandise value, take rate or advertising breakdown for Taobao and Tmall. Quick commerce losses, QwenWork E-commerce adoption, Qwen app usage and T-Head financials are not disclosed, and Alibaba says it cannot yet estimate the financial effect of the November 16 export rule.

Who: Alibaba Group Holding Limited, with Chief Executive Eddie Wu, Chief Financial Officer Toby Xu and Alibaba E-commerce Business Group Chief Executive Jiang Fan; the merchants and brands that sell and advertise on Taobao and Tmall.

What: Revenue rose 10% to RMB271.5 billion in the September quarter. Customer management revenue fell 5% to RMB75.0 billion, or grew 1% like-for-like once a program that books subsidies as contra revenue is excluded. Sales and marketing expenses fell 38% to RMB41.3 billion, AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue rose 53%, and adjusted EBITA rose 260%. Alibaba launched QwenWork E-commerce to automate merchant tasks including advertising, cut its next-year cloud growth target to 30% to 45%, and said a new US export rule will affect its access to compute outside China.
When: The results cover the three months ended September 30, 2026, and were announced on November 19, 2026, followed by an earnings call at 7:00 a.m. U.S. Eastern Time the same day.

Where: Announced in Hong Kong for Alibaba's NYSE and HKEX listings; the advertising and merchant figures relate to Taobao and Tmall in China, with international effects from AliExpress in the European Union.

Why: The figures show where Alibaba is putting its money. Merchant income on its Chinese marketplaces is roughly flat beneath an accounting change, reported marketing spend has fallen sharply as quick commerce subsidies shrink, and growth now comes from cloud and AI, where capital spending, chip supply and US export rules set the pace.
